summary: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart.
New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.

stories.title: A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
summary: A solar eclipse recorded more than 2,700 years ago is revealing surprising secrets about Earth's rotation and the Sun's ancient behavior.

By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital, scientists were able to reconstruct a total solar eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and obtain more accurate measurements of how fast Earth was spinning at the time.

stories.title: What do we still need to know about the Tyne nurdle spill?

stories.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
summary: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind.

Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

stories.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
summary: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures.
The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.

stories.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
summary: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids.
Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations.
Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.

stories.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
summary: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy.
Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away.
One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.

stories.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
summary: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water.
Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic.
Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.

stories.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
summary: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment.
In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.

stories.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia.

Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect.
The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.
